name: What We Ate: The Synthesis Transition and Its Erasures
description: A quietly devastating cultural documentary tracing the collapse of distinct culinary traditions across the Great Lakes corridor between 2140 and 2210, interviewing elderly residents across all tiers about food memories that have no living equivalent, interspersed with footage of synthesis production facilities that now supply over 94% of M88's caloric intake. The film treats food not as nutrition but as a form of memory architecture, arguing that the synthetic transition did not merely change what people eat but permanently altered how cultural identity is transmitted across generations. Directed by Maren Solís-Ekwueme, it took eleven years to produce.
cultural_impact: Sparked a significant revival of interest in pre-synthesis cooking among Tier 2-3 populations, contributing to the emergence of the Lakefire food festival circuit and a measurable increase in black-market agricultural ingredient trading.
story_hooks: One of the film's elderly interview subjects, a 104-year-old woman in the Outer Stack, mentions a specific dish her grandmother made — and a food historian realizes the recipe she describes contains an ingredient that should not have been available in that region at that time.
Solís-Ekwueme received a significant anonymous donation late in the production that she has never explained; someone wants to know where it came from.
A synthesis corporation executive privately contacts the director after the film's release — not to threaten her, but to confess something.
